_anchors.canvas.w: 58. The widest frame is the tuck's first: a scaleX of 1.17 on the root bone stretches the whole body sideways about the hips, so the head's far edge travels from 44 px out to 50. The silhouette lock found it — a part pixel reached column 47 of a 48 px cell with no room left for the outline ring. **A squash channel changes a sprite's bounding box and the cell has to be sized for the widest frame, not the rest pose.**
_anchors.canvas.h: 52. The body stands 34 px from ear tip to paw and the rise clip's stretch adds 3, with the outline ring and margin either side.
_anchors.canvas.originX: 24, and it is deliberately LEFT of centre. Every clip puts the head forward of the hips and the tail behind them, but the head is a 12 px mass and the tail is a taper: the painted body is not symmetric about its root.
_anchors.canvas.originY: 28, the hip joint. The scene anchors the cat by its lowest painted pixel rather than by this row, because the paws move between clips.
_anchors.tones.perMaterial: 5, the Chrono idiom he ranked first on 15/08 and the budget every subject in this project shares.
_anchors.frames.walk: 4, one per named phase. The tuck plays ONCE and holds its last frame, so nothing here is interpolated for smoothness across a loop point — every frame is a pose the eye stops on.
_anchors.light.x: -0.5, from the upper left, as every subject in this project except the astronaut.
_anchors.light.y: -0.72, and it is HIGHER than the moon's -0.5. This is late afternoon in a garden rather than a low sun on a plain: the light comes down through leaves, so the top of the animal is lit and the shelves cast their shadow downward.
_anchors.light.z: -0.3, slightly toward the viewer. A cat is a stack of round masses and a grazing light would spend the whole ramp on one flank; a little front light keeps the near side reading.
_anchors.light.curve: 1.1, near linear. The coat's own value range is wide, so the ramp does not need bending to keep the dark end off the floor.
_anchors.gait.swing: 0.3 turns, 108 degrees. Derived from the reach: a front paw goes from tucked under the chest to stretched above the head across one bounce, which is about 100 degrees of shoulder, and the keys are fractions of it.
_anchors.gait.lift: 5 px. The tuck drops the hips 3.5 px into the compression, which is a fifth of the standing hip height and reads as taking a landing.
_anchors.gait.depth: 6 px. Unused by all three clips, which are authored in the screen plane; it is here so the file is complete and so a future clip that throws a paw at the camera has an anchored amplitude to spend.
_anchors.body.scale: 1. The cat is 34 px in a 200 px world, which puts it at a sixth of the screen width — the proportion a vertical climber needs for the player to see two bands of shelves above the character.
_anchors.texture.speckle: 0. The 15/08 verdict retired per-pixel noise: it tied for last as part of the high-budget idiom.
_anchors.shadow.steps: 7, one more than the deepest mass here (the head, 5.6 of depth radius) so an ear can shade the skull behind it.
_anchors.shadow.strength: 1 ramp step, against the moon's 2. A garden scatters light into its own shadows and a vacuum does not, and this is that difference expressed as a number.
_anchors.fill.weight: 0.16, against the moon's 0.03. Same reason: bounce. An outdoor scene under leaves has a strong fill, and the declared cost — a fill compresses the value range — is affordable here because the coat's range is 36 to 205 and the moon's suit had nowhere to give.
_anchors.playback.msPerFrame: 55. Four frames make a 220 ms bounce. A cat's contact with a surface it springs off is about a fifth of a second, and anything longer reads as a pause rather than as a spring.
_anchors.playback.scale: 4, read only by the bench viewer. The game sets its own.
_anchors._why-a-second-file: A frame count lives in the tunables, and a clip that plays once needs a different one from a clip that loops. Everything else in this file is byte-identical to `cat.json` on purpose: the canvas, the origin, the light and the ramps must agree across the three clips or the animal changes size or lighting when its state changes.
_anchors.outline.enabled: true. The 15/08 ink verdict: a drawn line is half of what made the winning sample read. Every subject in this project has carried one since.
_anchors.outline.material: "ink". The palette's own line material, a warm dark brown rather than a black — a neutral line against a warm coat would be the one cool thing in the picture.
_anchors.outline.inner: true, and it is now doing almost nothing on this subject BY DESIGN. The flag is per sprite and can only say all-or-nothing; whether two shapes are one surface is a fact about those two shapes, so it is declared per part with `Part.weld`. Every solid on the cat is welded — a cat has no seams — and the inner line survives only where a welded part meets an unwelded one. Left true because the mechanism is the weld, not the switch, and turning the switch off would also silence a seam that ought to be there.
_anchors.outline.rim: false. `rim` and `enabled` are the two answers to the same question and this project settled on the drawn line on 15/08. Kept expressible so "both" and "neither" stay reachable.
_anchors.shadow.bias: 0.25, the project-wide value since run 7. Depth tolerance, so a curved surface does not shadow itself along its own tangent.
_anchors.fill.x: 0.45, opposite the key in x. A fill is what a photographer puts across from the key light and what a painter calls bounce.
_anchors.fill.y: 0.5, from BELOW. The key comes down through leaves and the bounce comes up off the ground, which is what an outdoor scene actually does.
_anchors.fill.z: -0.3, matching the key's own z. The fill is a weaker second lamp, not a different camera.
